---
title: "Projections and distances"
description: >
  Choosing a coordinate reference system that keeps distances accurate,
  summarising the distances between locations, and the empirical variogram.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "85%",
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)
```

A geostatistical model describes how the correlation between two locations
falls with the distance between them. Its scale parameter, `phi`, is a
distance, and so are the predictions' reach and the empirical variogram. The
distances must therefore be measured in a projected coordinate reference
system (CRS) that keeps them close to their true values on the Earth. This
article shows how RiskMap chooses such a CRS, how to check one, and how
distances enter the variogram and the model.

```{r load-data, message = FALSE}
library(RiskMap)
library(sf)

data(liberia)
liberia <- st_as_sf(liberia,
                    coords = c("long", "lat"),
                    crs = 4326)
```

## Choosing a projection

Longitude and latitude are angles, not distances. A degree of longitude spans
about 111 km at the equator and nothing at the poles. `propose_crs()` proposes
the projected CRS that keeps distances between the locations closest to their
values on the Earth. It proposes a WGS 84 UTM zone when one is nearly as good
as the best projection, as for Liberia.

```{r propose-crs}
crs <- propose_crs(liberia)
crs
```

`crs_distortion()` measures how much a CRS stretches or shrinks the distances
over the data. The UTM zone distorts them by a small fraction of a per cent,
while the Web Mercator projection of online maps (EPSG:3857) stretches them by
up to 1.8% this close to the equator, and by far more further from it.

```{r distortion}
crs_distortion(liberia, crs)
crs_distortion(liberia, 3857)
```

A region too wide for one UTM zone gets a conformal projection centred on the
data. These four points span almost 20 degrees of longitude and latitude.

```{r wide-region}
wide <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lon = c(12, 31, 12, 31),
                            lat = c(-13, -13, 5, 5)),
                 coords = c("lon", "lat"),
                 crs = 4326)
wide_crs <- propose_crs(wide)
wide_crs$Name
crs_distortion(wide, wide_crs)
```

The data are then projected once, and every later step measures distances in
that CRS.

```{r project-data}
liberia <- st_transform(liberia, crs)
```

## Distances between locations

`summarise_distance()` describes the distances between the locations, and
between each location and its nearest neighbour. They bound what the data can
say about the spatial correlation. A scale much shorter than the distance to
the nearest neighbour, or much longer than the largest distance, can't be
estimated well.

```{r summarise-distance}
summarise_distance(liberia)
```

## The empirical variogram

The empirical variogram shows how the difference between two observations grows
with the distance between them. For binomial data it is computed on the
empirical logit of prevalence, which `elogit()` gives.

```{r variogram}
liberia$elogit <- elogit(liberia$npos, liberia$ntest)
set.seed(2026)
liberia_variogram <- variogram(liberia, variable = "elogit")
liberia_variogram
plot(liberia_variogram)
```

The band is a permutation envelope, the range of variograms that the data
would show if their values were shuffled among the locations, that is with no
spatial correlation, and points outside it are drawn in red. Points below the
band at short distances, where nearby villages are more alike than shuffled
pairs, point to spatial correlation, as the red points do here.
`plot_variogram()` takes further arguments, for example to show the number of
pairs of locations in each distance bin.

```{r variogram-pairs}
plot_variogram(liberia_variogram, show_pairs = TRUE)
```

## Distances in the model

`glgpm()` measures distances in the CRS of the data. Data in longitude and
latitude are projected to the CRS from `propose_crs()`, with a message naming
it. `distance_crs` sets the CRS explicitly, and `distance_units` chooses
kilometres, the default, or metres for `phi`. The two fits below are the same
model, with the logarithm of elevation as a covariate, and give the scale in
kilometres and in metres.

```{r fit-units}
set.seed(2026)
fit_km <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
                data = liberia,
                family = "binomial",
                denominator = ntest,
                distance_crs = crs,
                messages = FALSE)
set.seed(2026)
fit_m <- glgpm(npos ~ log_elevation + gp(),
               data = liberia,
               family = "binomial",
               denominator = ntest,
               distance_crs = crs,
               distance_units = "m",
               messages = FALSE)
c(km = coef(fit_km)$phi, m = coef(fit_m)$phi)
```

For the exponential correlation, the default `kappa = 0.5` of `gp()`, the
correlation falls to 0.05 at a distance of $\log(20)\phi \approx 3\phi$, the
practical range.

```{r practical-range}
log(20) * coef(fit_km)$phi
```

`variogram()`, `summarise_distance()`, `create_grid()` and `specify_glgpm()`
take the same `distance_crs` and `distance_units`, so that every distance in an
analysis is measured as the fit's are.

Chapter [2](https://www.mbgr.org/02_handling-spatial-data.html) of the book
*Model-based geostatistics for global public health using R* treats spatial
data in R, from coordinate reference systems to covariates and prediction
grids, and Chapter [3](https://www.mbgr.org/03_model-fitting.html) the
variogram and the spatial correlation.
